products.name: First Flush Whole Leaf
products.description: The first pluck of spring, whole leaf: bright, floral, and carrying the muscatel character Darjeeling first flush is famous for.
products.longDescription: The first flush is a race against the sun: leaves picked in the earliest weeks after winter dormancy, when the bush has stored a season's worth of aromatics. Grown above 3,500 ft in Darjeeling, withered long and fired light, this tea brews pale gold rather than red. Each pack is whole leaf, light in the cup, and best drunk without milk so nothing stands between you and the spring.

brewingGuide.notes: Skip the milk. First flush is prized for its bright muscatel aromatics, and a slightly cooler pour keeps them intact.

products.name: First Flush Broken Leaf
products.description: Broken-leaf Darjeeling first flush: the same spring character with a quicker, stronger brew.
products.longDescription: Same garden, same pluck, smaller cut. Breaking the leaf exposes more surface to the water, so a broken-leaf first flush gives up its colour and briskness in half the time a whole leaf takes. You keep the muscatel note and trade a little of the floral top end for body. It is the everyday Darjeeling for people who find whole leaf too delicate for a morning cup.

brewingGuide.notes: Broken leaf brews faster and stronger than whole leaf, so shorten the steep rather than the leaf.

products.name: First Flush Broken Mixed
products.description: A robust mixed broken grade from the Darjeeling spring harvest: strong, brisk, and happy to take milk.
products.longDescription: From warmer, lower slopes in the Darjeeling foothills, where the bush wakes earlier and grows faster. That makes a bolder, maltier cup with more colour and less of the ethereal floral note you get at altitude, which is exactly what you want in a tea that has to stand up to milk and sugar. The most versatile grade we sell, and the best value per cup.

brewingGuide.notes: A full boil and a longer steep bring out the malty depth, and this grade takes milk happily.

products.name: First Flush Fannings
products.description: Fine Darjeeling first flush fannings: fast-brewing and full-strength. The working tea of the Darjeeling hills.
products.longDescription: Fannings are the finest cut: the smallest particles sifted from the same first flush pluck. More surface area means near-instant extraction, a deep coppery colour, and a cup with real backbone. This is not a contemplative tea and does not pretend to be. It is the grade the hills actually drink every morning, and it makes the best masala chai in the catalogue.

brewingGuide.notes: Fannings brew fast and strong, so watch the clock, or lean in and make masala chai.

products.name: First Flush
products.description: The first pluck of spring: a bright, floral Darjeeling with the light muscatel lift the season is known for.
products.longDescription:
First flush is the first picking of the year, taken in the weeks after the tea bushes wake from winter. The new shoots are small and tender, and they carry the aromatics the plant has stored through the cold months. That is why a first flush Darjeeling tastes so unlike other black teas: lighter, greener and more fragrant.

It brews a pale gold rather than a deep red. The aroma is fresh and floral, the body is light, and the finish carries the gentle muscatel lift (a bright, grape-like note) that Darjeeling spring teas are known for. There is a little briskness at the edges, but nothing heavy.

Drink it plain, without milk or sugar, so the delicate notes come through. It suits a slow morning or a mid-afternoon cup, and goes well with light food such as butter biscuits, fruit or a plain sponge. The leaf gives a good second steep; add about 30 seconds to the time.

brewingGuide.notes: Skip the milk. A slightly cooler pour keeps the bright spring aromatics intact.

products.name: Golden Needle
products.description: Golden-tipped buds that brew a rounded, honeyed cup, the richest tea in the range.
products.longDescription:
Golden Needle is made almost entirely from young buds. As they are rolled and oxidised, the fine hairs on the buds turn a deep gold, which gives the tea its name and its look: slender, twisted golden tips.

Because buds are rich and tender, this is the fullest cup in our range. It brews a clear amber with an aroma of honey and baked bread. The taste is smooth and rounded, with a malty depth and a natural sweetness that needs no sugar. There is very little bitterness, even if you steep it a little long.

Try the first cup plain to taste the honeyed character; it is sturdy enough for a splash of milk if you prefer. It holds up well to a second and third steep, so a little leaf goes a long way. A fine choice for a special occasion, or as a gift for someone who loves black tea.

brewingGuide.notes: Rich enough to take a splash of milk, but try the first cup plain.

products.name: Green Tea
products.description: Unoxidised Darjeeling leaf: fresh, grassy and gentle, for an everyday lighter cup.
products.longDescription:
Green tea is the least changed form of the tea leaf. Soon after picking, the leaves are heated to stop oxidation, the natural process that turns leaves dark and gives black tea its colour and strength. The leaf stays green, and the cup keeps the fresh character of the plant.

It brews a pale yellow-green cup with a clean, grassy aroma. The taste is fresh and gentle, with a soft vegetal sweetness and a clean finish. It is lighter in body and less astringent than our black teas, which makes it an easy cup to drink through the day.

Temperature matters most with green tea. Water straight off the boil scorches the leaf and draws out bitterness, so let the kettle rest for a few minutes first. Drink it plain, without milk. It pairs well with light meals, and the leaf can be steeped three times; the later cups are softer and sweeter.

brewingGuide.notes: Let boiled water rest for a few minutes first. Too hot and the cup turns bitter.

products.name: Pan Roasted
products.description: Leaf fired in a hot pan by hand, giving a toasty, nutty green tea with a soft finish.
products.longDescription:
Pan Roasted is a green tea finished over fire. Instead of being steamed, the freshly picked leaf is tossed in a hot pan to stop oxidation. The heat dries the leaf and gives it a warm, toasted character you will not find in a steamed green tea.

The cup is golden-green, with a nutty aroma like lightly toasted grain or chestnut. Beneath the roast the fresh green notes are still there, and the finish is soft and rounded rather than grassy. It is gentler than most green teas, with very little bitterness.

Brew it a few degrees hotter than other green teas, around 85°C, to bring out the roasted notes, and drink it plain. Its warmth makes it a good green tea for cooler evenings and for anyone who finds regular green tea too grassy. It pairs well with savoury food.

brewingGuide.notes: A little hotter than other green teas brings out the roasted notes.

products.name: Silver Needle
products.description: Downy silver buds, simply withered and dried, the most delicate cup we make.
products.longDescription:
Silver Needle is made only from the unopened leaf bud, picked before it unfurls. Each bud is covered in fine silver-white down. The buds are simply withered and dried, with no rolling and almost no processing, so what you brew is very close to the bud as it grew on the bush.

The cup is very pale, almost clear, with a delicate aroma of fresh hay and soft flowers. The taste is light, smooth and subtly sweet, with no bitterness. It is the most delicate tea we make, and its flavour builds slowly over a long steep and several infusions.

Give it time and cooler water. The buds are light and bulky, so use about 2 teaspoons per cup and steep for 4–5 minutes at around 80°C. Drink it plain. It rewards a quiet moment and a clean palate, and the buds can be steeped three or four times.

brewingGuide.notes: The buds are bulky, so use more by volume and a longer steep than you would for black tea.

products.name: White Tea
products.description: Gently withered leaf and bud: soft, sweet and lightly floral.
products.longDescription:
White tea is handled as little as possible. The leaf and bud are left to wither naturally and are then dried, without the rolling and oxidation that make black tea. The result keeps much of the freshness and sweetness of the living leaf.

It brews a pale golden cup with a soft floral aroma. The taste is mellow and gently sweet, with a light body and a smooth, clean finish. Because it includes leaf as well as bud, it has a little more body than Silver Needle while staying delicate.

Keep the water below boiling, around 80°C, and do not rush the steep. Drink it plain. It is a calm, light cup for the afternoon or evening, and it rewards several short steeps, each one a little different from the last.

brewingGuide.notes: Keep the water below boiling and do not rush it.

products.name: Whole Leaf 1st Flush
products.description: Unbroken spring leaves, picked by hand, the fullest expression of a Darjeeling first flush.
products.longDescription:
This is first flush Darjeeling with the leaf left whole. The leaves are picked by hand and kept intact through withering, rolling and drying, rather than broken into smaller pieces. Whole leaves release their flavour slowly, so the cup has more layers than a broken grade.

It brews a bright, pale gold. The aroma is fresh and floral, and the taste opens with spring flowers, moves into the muscatel note Darjeeling is known for, and ends with a long, clean finish. It is light in body but full of flavour, with a gentle briskness.

Use a little more leaf by volume than usual, as whole leaves are bulky, and watch them unfurl in the pot. Drink it plain. This is the cup to choose when you want to taste a first flush at its best, and the leaf gives a fine second steep.

brewingGuide.notes: Whole leaves are bulky, so use a little more by volume, and drink it plain.

products.name: 2nd Flush
products.description: The summer pluck: a deeper, fruitier Darjeeling with the classic muscatel character.
products.longDescription:
Second flush is the summer picking, taken in early summer once the spring growth has passed. The leaves are larger and more mature than in spring, and the warmer weather gives them a deeper, fuller flavour.

The cup is a rich amber. The aroma is fruity, and the taste brings ripe fruit and the muscatel character (a grape-like sweetness) that made second flush Darjeeling famous. It has more body and strength than a first flush, with a smooth, lingering finish.

Try the first cup plain to taste the muscatel; it is sturdy enough to take a splash of milk if you prefer. A good all-day black tea, and a fine match for breakfast or an afternoon snack.

brewingGuide.notes: Sturdy enough for a splash of milk, but try the first cup plain.

products.name: 3rd Flush
products.description: The autumn pluck: a mellow, rounded cup with a coppery colour and a gentle sweetness.
products.longDescription:
Third flush, also called autumn flush, is picked after the monsoon as the growing season winds down. The bushes grow more slowly in the cooler weather, and the leaf develops a softer, rounder character than the summer teas.

It brews a coppery, reddish cup. The aroma is warm and gentle, and the taste is mellow and smooth, with a light natural sweetness and low astringency. It is easy to drink and forgiving, even if you steep it a little long.

Drink it plain or with milk; it takes both well. It makes a dependable everyday cup, morning or afternoon, and is a good introduction to Darjeeling for anyone used to stronger tea.

brewingGuide.notes: Takes milk well, and holds up to a slightly longer steep.

products.name: Whole Leaf 2nd Flush
products.description: Unbroken summer leaves for a fuller, fruitier muscatel cup. Arriving soon.
products.longDescription:
Whole Leaf 2nd Flush is our summer Darjeeling with the leaf kept whole. The leaves are left intact through rolling and drying, so they open fully in the pot and release their flavour slowly.

Expect a rich amber cup with ripe fruit and the muscatel sweetness that second flush is known for, with more body and a longer finish than the broken grade. Drink it plain, or with a splash of milk.

brewingGuide.notes: Whole leaves are bulky, so use a little more by volume. Try the first cup plain.

products.name: Whole Leaf Autumn Flush
products.description: Unbroken autumn leaves for a smooth, coppery, gently sweet cup. Arriving soon.
products.longDescription:
Whole Leaf Autumn Flush is our autumn Darjeeling with the leaf kept whole. Picked as the growing season winds down, the leaves stay intact so they unfurl fully and give a smooth, layered cup.

Expect a coppery cup that is mellow and gently sweet, with low astringency and a soft, rounded finish. It is easy to drink plain and takes milk well.

brewingGuide.notes: Forgiving and mellow, and takes milk well.

products.name: Chamomile
products.description: Whole chamomile flowers for a calm, honeyed, caffeine-free cup. Arriving soon.
products.longDescription:
Our Chamomile is made from whole dried chamomile flowers rather than broken pieces or dust. Whole flowers keep more of their natural oils, which gives a fuller flavour and aroma.

It brews a clear golden cup with a sweet, floral aroma and a hint of apple. The taste is soft and honeyed, with no bitterness. Chamomile is naturally caffeine-free, which makes it a popular choice for the evening.

Pour water just off the boil and steep for about 5 minutes, or longer for a stronger cup. Drink it plain or with a little honey.

brewingGuide.notes: Cover the cup while it steeps to keep the aroma in.

gardens.name: Gopaldhara
story: Gopaldhara sits above Mirik, and its upper sections are among the highest planted land in Darjeeling, rising past 7,000 feet. Altitude is the whole story here: at that height the bush grows slowly, the internodes shorten, and the leaf concentrates the aromatics that give Darjeeling first flush its muscatel signature.

The first flush is a narrow window. After winter dormancy the bushes push a small quantity of tender two-leaves-and-a-bud, and the pluck runs for a few weeks in late February through April. That leaf is withered long and fired light, which is why a first flush brews pale gold rather than red, and why it should never meet milk.

gardens.name: Rohini
story: Rohini lies lower down the hill, on warmer slopes where the Darjeeling foothills heat up earlier in the season. Lower elevation means the bushes wake sooner, so Rohini is often among the first gardens in the district to send out a first flush at all.
A warmer, faster-growing leaf makes a bolder cup: more body, more malt, less of the ethereal floral top note you get at 7,000 feet.
Nothing here is blended with leaf from outside the district.

journal.title: Reading the Seasons: First, Second and Autumn Flush
journal.excerpt: One garden can give you three very different teas in a single year. A simple guide to what each flush tastes like, and how to brew it.
journal.imageAlt: A Darjeeling tea garden seen through pine branches
journal.author: The Elegant Sip Tasting Team
body: Darjeeling is one of the few places where the calendar is written into the tea. The same bushes, on the same slopes, give very different leaf as the year turns, and the name of a Darjeeling tea usually tells you when it was picked before it tells you anything else. Learn to read the seasons and the whole range starts to make sense.
Each picking season is called a flush: the burst of new growth a tea bush sends out after a rest. A Darjeeling garden has several a year, and each one tastes of the weather that grew it.

The first flush comes after winter. Through the cold months the bushes are dormant, and when the days lengthen they push out a small amount of tender growth, picked as two leaves and a bud. Depending on the garden and the year, the pluck runs from late February into April. This is the lightest and most fragrant tea of the year: pale gold in the cup, floral and bright, with a crisp edge and a light muscatel lift.

That brightness comes partly from the leaf and partly from how it is made. First flush is withered for a long time and fired lightly, so much of the fresh spring character survives. It is also why the dry tea looks the way it does, a mix of green and brown leaf rather than the even dark colour you might expect from a black tea.

Brew first flush at about 90 °C, not a rolling boil, for 3 to 4 minutes, and drink it plain. Milk covers exactly the delicate notes you are paying for. Our First Flush and Whole Leaf 1st Flush are both spring teas. The whole leaf version keeps the leaves unbroken, so use a little more of it by volume.

The second flush follows in early summer, roughly May into June, after the bushes have had a short rest. The weather is warmer, the leaf grows a little faster, and the tea it makes is deeper and fuller. In the cup it turns amber rather than gold, with ripe fruit and the grape-like muscatel note that Darjeeling is famous for.

Second flush is sturdier than first flush, so it takes hotter water: about 95 °C for 3 to 4 minutes. It is lovely plain and strong enough for a splash of milk if you like one, though we suggest tasting the first cup without. Our 2nd Flush is this tea.

Between the second flush and the autumn harvest comes the monsoon. Heavy rain makes the bushes grow quickly, and the leaf picked in these months generally goes into stronger, everyday teas rather than the delicate grades. We do not sell a monsoon flush, but it explains the gap in the calendar.

The autumn flush arrives once the rains clear, usually October into November. The air turns dry and cool, the bushes slow down before winter, and the leaf makes a mellow, rounded tea with a coppery colour and a gentle sweetness. It has less of the spring sparkle and more comfort.
Autumn flush is the most forgiving of the three. Brew it at about 95 °C for 3 to 4 minutes. It holds up to a slightly longer steep and takes milk well. Our 3rd Flush is the autumn tea.

If you want to taste the difference for yourself, brew a first, second and autumn flush side by side, with the same amount of leaf and the right temperature for each. Look at the colour first, from pale gold to amber to copper. Then smell the wet leaf before you sip. Most people find the jump from first to second flush the most surprising, because it is the same plant, and often the same garden, only a couple of months apart.

A simple way to choose: if you like light, fragrant teas and drink them without milk, start with first flush. If you want a fuller cup with that classic muscatel character, try second flush. If you want something smooth and easygoing for the afternoon, with or without milk, reach for autumn flush.
Because each flush is a harvest and not a recipe, every lot is a little different from the year before. That is not a flaw. It is the reason to drink Darjeeling by the season.

journal.title: Why Altitude Shapes the Cup
journal.excerpt: Cool nights, thin air and slow growth. What height does to a tea leaf, and why so much of the best Darjeeling is grown high up.
journal.imageAlt: A tea garden on a Darjeeling ridge lined with tall pines
journal.author: The Elegant Sip Tasting Team
body: Ask anyone who grows tea in Darjeeling what makes the district special, and the answer usually starts with height. Gardens here are planted on steep hillsides, from warm valleys to ridges several thousand feet up, and that range of altitude shows up in the cup as clearly as the season does.

Higher up, the air is thinner and cooler, the nights are colder, and mist settles over the slopes for much of the day. A tea bush in those conditions grows slowly. New shoots take longer to form, the gaps between the leaves on a stem get shorter, and the leaf has more time to build up the compounds that give tea its aroma.

Slow growth also means less leaf. A high garden produces less tea than one lower down, and the pluck has to be more patient. In return the leaf tends to be more fragrant, more layered and more delicate. This is the floral, muscatel lift people associate with the finest Darjeeling.

Gopaldhara is a good example. It sits above Mirik, and its upper sections rise past 7,000 feet, among the highest planted land in Darjeeling. At that height the bushes grow slowly and the leaf concentrates its aromatics, and the first flush that comes from them is pale, bright and full of perfume. It is the kind of tea to brew carefully and drink plain.

Lower down, the picture changes. Rohini lies on warmer slopes in the Darjeeling foothills, between about 1,500 and 4,500 feet. The bushes there wake earlier in the year, so Rohini is often among the first gardens in the district to pick a first flush at all. The leaf grows faster and makes a bolder cup, with more body and malt and less of the ethereal top note you find at 7,000 feet.

Neither is better in every way. A high-grown tea is not simply a stronger or weaker version of a low-grown one. They are different teas. High gardens are prized for fragrance and finesse. Lower gardens give depth, colour and strength, which is exactly what you want in a cup that has to stand up to milk.

Altitude is not the only thing at work. The direction a slope faces decides how much sun it gets, the soil changes from one section of a garden to the next, and the weather in a particular year can move a harvest earlier or later. Two gardens at the same height can still taste different. But if you want a single clue to how a Darjeeling will drink before you open the pack, height is a good one.

It also tells you how to brew. A delicate, high-grown first flush is happiest at around 90 °C with no milk, while a fuller tea can take hotter water and a splash of milk. The brewing card on each of our product pages gives the exact numbers for that tea.
Our Gardens page has more about Gopaldhara and Rohini, and each tea page names its garden once that lot is confirmed. Once you know where a tea grew, you start to taste the hillside in it.

journal.title: Keeping Your Tea Fresh at Home
journal.excerpt: Light, air, heat and strong smells are what fade a good tea. A few easy habits that keep every cup tasting the way it did on day one.
journal.imageAlt: An Elegant Sip tea box with the snow-capped Himalaya behind it
journal.author: The Elegant Sip Tasting Team
body: Good tea does not go off the way milk does, but it does fade. The aromas that make a Darjeeling worth drinking are delicate, and over time they drift away until the cup tastes flat and papery. The good news is that keeping tea fresh at home comes down to a few easy habits.
Four things wear tea down: light, air, heat and strong smells. Moisture is a fifth, and the most damaging if it gets in.

Light breaks down the compounds that carry flavour and colour, which is why tea should never live in a clear glass jar on a sunny shelf, however nice it looks. Our teas are packed in light-proof packaging for exactly this reason, so the simplest option is often to keep the tea in the pack it came in.

Air slowly takes the aroma away. Press as much air out of the pack as you can before you close it, and close it properly every time. If you move tea into another container, choose one that is airtight and not much bigger than the tea inside, so there is less air around the leaf.
Heat speeds all of this up. Keep tea somewhere cool and dark; a cupboard is ideal. Avoid the shelf above the kettle or the stove, and anywhere that warms up in the afternoon sun.

Tea leaves soak up smells very easily. That is how scented teas are made, and it is also why a pack stored next to spices or coffee can end up tasting of them. Give your tea its own corner of the cupboard, away from anything strongly scented.

Keep it dry, too. Always use a dry spoon, and do not store tea in the fridge or freezer. Every time you take it out, the cold leaf draws moisture from the warm kitchen air, and damp leaf loses its flavour quickly.

It helps to buy amounts you will drink while the tea is at its best, rather than stocking up for a year. Lighter teas such as first flush, green and white teas are the most fragile, so drink those first. Fuller black teas, such as second and autumn flush, are a little more robust.
Every one of our packs has its pack date printed on it, so you always know how long a tea has been sealed. We pack in small batches close to harvest, so that the clock starts as late as possible.

If a tea you have kept for a while tastes dull, try brewing it with a little more leaf before you give up on it. But the best fix is prevention. A cool, dark cupboard, a closed pack and a dry spoon will keep every cup close to how it tasted on the day you opened it.

journal.title: The Art of the First Flush
journal.excerpt: The first harvest of spring is a race against the sun. Why the earliest pluck of the year commands the highest prices, and the most patience.
journal.author: The Elegant Sip Tasting Team
journal.imageAlt: Fresh tea shoots catching the early morning sun
body: Every spring the tea gardens of Darjeeling wake up after months of rest, and for a few weeks the whole district works to the rhythm of the first flush. It is the most anticipated harvest of the year, one of the smallest and often the most expensive, and it makes a tea unlike anything else Darjeeling produces.

Through the winter the bushes are dormant. The cold slows them almost to a stop, and they store up energy for the year ahead. When the days lengthen and warm, that energy goes into the first new growth of the season: small, tender shoots that are picked as two leaves and a bud.

The window is narrow. Depending on the garden and the weather, the first flush runs from late February into April, and each section of a garden has to be picked at the right moment. Leave the shoots a few days too long in the warming sun and they grow coarse, and the delicacy that makes a first flush special is lost. That is the race against the sun.

The pluck is done by hand. Pluckers move along the terraces taking only the youngest shoots, and return to the same bushes as new ones appear. It is slow, skilled work, and it yields only a small amount of tea.

In the factory, first flush is handled gently. The fresh leaf is spread out and withered for a long time until it is soft enough to roll without breaking, then rolled, left to oxidise only briefly and fired lightly. Because the oxidation is short and the firing light, much of the leaf stays green, and the finished tea is a mix of green and brown rather than an even dark colour.

In the cup, that gentle making shows as a pale gold liquor and a bright, floral aroma, with a crisp, lively edge and a light muscatel lift. It is closer in feel to a fine white or green tea than to the strong black tea many people grew up with.

Why does it cost more? Partly because there is so little of it: the bushes have only just woken, and the yield from those first weeks is small. Partly because of the care it takes, from the hand pluck to the long wither. And partly because it is the first fresh tea of the year, so everyone wants it. When a lot of first flush is gone, it is gone until next spring.

First flush asks for patience in the cup as well. Brew it at about 90 °C rather than with boiling water, which scorches its delicate aromatics, and steep it for 3 to 4 minutes. Use about a teaspoon per cup, or a little more by volume for whole leaf. Then drink it plain, because milk buries exactly the character that makes it worth buying. Good first flush leaf will give you a second steep, and often a third.

We offer it in two styles. First Flush is the classic spring tea, and Whole Leaf 1st Flush keeps the leaves unbroken for the fullest expression of the season. Both are packed in small batches close to harvest, with the pack date printed on every pack, so you can taste the spring as close as possible to the morning it was picked.

journal.title: A Field Guide to Steeping
journal.excerpt: Temperature, time, leaf amount, and the often-misunderstood art of the re-steep. Everything you need to stop guessing and start tasting.
journal.author: The Elegant Sip Tasting Team
journal.imageAlt: A freshly brewed cup beside a jar of Morning Dew on a hillside ledge
body: Most disappointing cups of tea are not the tea's fault. Good leaf brewed too hot, too long or without care can taste bitter, flat or thin, and the same leaf brewed well can be a revelation. You do not need special equipment to get it right. You need four things under control: how much leaf, how hot the water, how long it steeps, and what you do with the leaves afterwards.

Start with the leaf. Use about one teaspoon of leaf per 240 ml cup of water for most teas. Bulky teas need more by volume: whole leaf teas take about one and a half teaspoons, and white teas, which are mostly fluffy buds, take about two. If you have kitchen scales, weighing is more reliable than spooning, because large leaves and buds take up far more room than they weigh.

Temperature matters more than anything else. Boiling water suits some teas and is harsh on others. White and green teas want about 80 °C. Pan-roasted green tea is happier at 85 °C, which brings out its toasty notes. First flush and Golden Needle want about 90 °C, and second and autumn flush can take 95 °C.

You do not need a thermometer. Boil the kettle, then let it stand with the lid open. After a minute or two it will be somewhere around 90 °C, and after about five minutes it will be close to 80 °C. If your kettle has temperature settings, use them. Pouring boiling water straight onto a delicate tea is the most common reason it tastes bitter.

Then time it. Black teas steep for 3 to 4 minutes, green teas for 2 to 3, and white teas for 3 to 5. Use a timer rather than guessing. An extra minute does not make tea stronger in a good way. It makes it astringent, with that drying, puckering feel at the back of the mouth. If you want a stronger cup, add more leaf, not more time.

Give the leaves room. Whole leaves unfurl as they steep and need space to open fully, so a teapot or a roomy infuser basket works better than a small tea ball that packs them tight. When the time is up, lift the leaves out or pour off all the tea, so it does not keep steeping in the pot.

Decide about milk before you brew. First flush, white and green teas are best plain, because milk covers the delicate character that makes them worth buying. Second flush, autumn flush and Golden Needle are sturdier and can take a splash of milk, though it is worth tasting the first cup without.

Then there is the re-steep, the most misunderstood part of brewing. Good whole leaf tea is meant to be steeped more than once. The first steep is the introduction. The second is often the best cup of the session, as the leaves open fully and give up flavours they held back the first time.

Black teas usually give 2 to 3 steeps, green teas about 3, and white teas 3 to 4. For each new steep, use water at the same temperature and add roughly 30 seconds to the time. Stop when the cup starts to taste thin. Re-steeping is not about making tea go further. It is how the leaf is meant to be drunk.

Once you have the basics, adjust to your own taste, one thing at a time. If a tea tastes harsh, try slightly cooler water or a shorter steep. If it tastes weak, add a little more leaf. Change only one thing at a time, so you learn what each one does.

You do not have to remember all of this. Every one of our product pages carries a brewing card with the temperature, time, leaf amount and number of steeps for that tea, and our Brewing Guide puts it all in one place. Start from the card, then let your own cup be the final judge.

journal.title: From Mist to Cup: Our Sourcing Journey
journal.excerpt: No auction houses, no middlemen, no anonymity. How we built direct relationships with the gardens that grow the leaves we sell.
journal.author: The Elegant Sip Tasting Team
journal.imageAlt: Pluckers at work on a Darjeeling tea slope under heavy clouds
body: Most tea reaches you without a name. It is sold as a number in an auction lot, blended with leaf from many other gardens, graded by brokers and passed through several hands before it reaches a shop. By the time it is in your cup, nobody can tell you which hillside it grew on or who picked it. Elegant Sip exists to do the opposite.

The auction system is good at moving large amounts of tea, but it has two costs. The first is anonymity: once a garden's leaf is blended into a lot, its character disappears into an average. The second is fairness. With so many steps between the bush and the buyer, the person who grew the tea is usually the last one paid.

So we built the kind of supply chain we wanted to buy from. Our buyers work on the ground in the tea gardens of Darjeeling through the harvest seasons. They taste from the withering racks, walk the terraces and buy whole lots directly from the estates, with no auction house and no middleman in between.

Buying direct is not charity. It is quality control. When a grower is paid properly for good tea, they can pick at the perfect moment rather than the most profitable one, and take the extra care that fine leaf needs. That care is what you taste in the cup.

Choosing a lot starts with tasting. Every season brings different leaf, so we taste as the tea is made and buy the lots that show their garden and season clearly: the bright, floral lift of a high-grown first flush, the fuller muscatel of a second flush, the mellow sweetness of an autumn tea.

Once we buy a lot, we keep it as it is. We never blend leaf from different estates, so the tea you receive is what that garden produced, not a house blend built to taste the same every year. Each harvest is a little different, and that is part of the point.

Two of the gardens we buy from are on our Gardens page. Gopaldhara sits above Mirik, with sections rising past 7,000 feet, and gives slow-grown, fragrant leaf. Rohini lies lower, on warmer slopes in the foothills, and makes bolder teas with more body. We name a garden on a tea's page only once that lot is confirmed, because we would rather leave a detail out than guess.

Our teas are packed in small batches close to harvest, in light-proof packaging that shields the leaf from the light and air that fade it. The pack date is printed on every pack, so you always know how fresh your tea is.

The last step is yours. Every product page carries a brewing card with the temperature, steep time, leaf amount and number of steeps that suit that tea, so the care taken on the hillside is not undone by a kettle that is too hot.

We try to be just as straightforward about what we do not know. If a detail about a lot is not confirmed, we do not publish it. If a tea is not in stock yet, it is marked as coming soon rather than dressed up as available. Knowing where your tea comes from only means something if every part of the story is true.

From the mist on the terraces to the cup on your table, that is the journey: fewer hands, more care and a name on every tea. We think tea tastes better that way, and we think the people who grow it deserve to be known.
